title: The Fungal Internet Under Your Feet
hook: Scientists made the first global map of the underground fungal networks that feed most plants on Earth — a living web that quietly helps lock carbon into the soil.
key_points: Most land plants trade sugar to soil fungi for water and nutrients through their roots.
These mycorrhizal threads link plant to plant, weaving vast underground networks.
Researchers estimate the global web stretches on the order of 110 quadrillion kilometers.
They estimate it channels roughly 4 billion tons of CO2 into soils each year.
That makes these fungi major, long-overlooked players in climate and plant health.
content_html: Pull up almost any plant and you'll find its roots tangled with fungal threads. This is a mycorrhiza — an ancient partnership in which a plant feeds sugar to soil fungi, and the fungi repay it with water and nutrients their fine filaments reach far better than roots can. Those filaments don't stop at one plant: they link neighbor to neighbor, weaving a hidden underground web sometimes called the "wood wide web." Scientists have now, via ScienceDaily, mapped this network across the whole planet for the first time.
extra_html: The scale is hard to picture. Researchers estimate the global tangle of fungal threads stretches on the order of 110 quadrillion kilometers, and that it pulls roughly 4 billion tons of carbon dioxide down into soils every year. That last figure is why the work matters beyond botany: by moving carbon from plants into the ground, these fungi act as a giant, largely ignored lever on the climate, while also propping up the plants that feed nearly every land ecosystem. The map gives scientists a first real baseline for where these networks are richest — and where losing them could quietly hurt both crops and carbon storage.

related.title: Symbiosis
related.hook: Living things rarely go it alone. From gut microbes to coral reefs, species often share their lives — sometimes helping, sometimes harming, their partners.

related.title: Nutrient Cycles
related.hook: The carbon in your breath, the nitrogen in your DNA, the water in your blood — all of it has cycled through living things and the planet countless times. Nothing is used up; everything is recycled.

related.title: Why Plants Run the Planet
related.hook: Nearly every breath you take and every meal you eat traces back to plants — they make the oxygen, anchor the food chain, and lock away carbon for the whole biosphere.

related.title: What Are Fungi?
related.hook: Mushrooms, molds, and yeast belong to their own kingdom — not plants, not animals — and they make their living by digesting the world around them.

flashcards.prompt: What do plants and mycorrhizal fungi exchange with each other?
flashcards.back_html: Plants hand the fungi sugars made by photosynthesis; in return the fungal threads deliver water and nutrients drawn from the soil.

flashcards.prompt: Why do researchers call these fungal networks important for the climate?

choices.text: They channel roughly 4 billion tons of CO2 into soils each year
They cool the air by releasing water vapor
They reflect sunlight back into space

flashcards.explanation_html: The study estimates the networks move about 4 billion tons of carbon dioxide into the soil annually, making them a major, long-overlooked part of the carbon cycle.

flashcards.prompt: What was new about this 2026 study?

choices.text: It produced the first global map of these underground networks
It discovered that fungi exist underground
It proved plants don't need fungi at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Mycorrhizal partnerships were already well known; the advance was mapping the hidden global network for the first time and estimating its staggering scale.
